\begin{document}

\title[Decomposing the Attractor of Quantum-Behaved PSO]{Decomposing the Attractor of Quantum-Behaved PSO: What Random Weights, Bio-Inspired Leaders and Weight Scheduling Each Contribute}

\author*[1]{\sur{Manav}}\email{manav-ug23@nsut.ac.in} % const
\affil*[1]{\orgdiv{Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering},
\orgname{Netaji Subhas University of Technology}, \orgaddress{\city{Delhi}, \country{India}}}

\abstract{Quantum-behaved particle swarm optimization (QPSO) samples around an attractor that
mixes personal and global bests with a random weight. Hybrids often change this attractor in
several ways at once, so it is unclear which change matters. We separate four: replacing the
random weight with fixed weights, adding scout restarts, adding a ring-neighborhood ant or bee
leader as a third anchor, and scheduling that anchor's weight. Thirteen algorithms, including
L-SHADE, share one implementation and seeds, with a decision rule specified before the analysis.
Fixed weights are worse than QPSO on \DcRandomToFixedClWorse{} of \EoneN{} classical functions, and scouts at
their default limit are worse on \DcScoutsClWorse{} of \EoneN{} classical and \DcScoutsCeWorse{} of \EthreeN{} CEC2017 functions. The ant leader
is credited on \EtwoBioCountAnt{} of \EoneN{} and \EtwocBioCountAnt{} of \EthreeN, and the bee leader on \EtwoBioCountBee{} of \EoneN{} and \EtwocBioCountBee{} of \EthreeN; neither reaches the CEC2017 threshold. No schedule is
credited on any function. Moving the optimum away from the origin drops GWO from rank
\EoneRankGWO{} to \EonebRankGWO. At the standard CEC2017 budget, L-SHADE ranks first at $D=30$ and $D=50$.
Some ant-leader variants are better than QPSO on function means under Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests
(\EthreesThirtyBioPwBetterList{} at $D=30$, \EthreesFiftyBioPwBetterList{} at $D=50$), but not under the Nemenyi test, which we treat
as weak evidence. In feature selection, no BioQPSO variant gains on
QPSO, and all features are best on \FsAllBeatsList. The three-term attractor gives at most a small
gain over QPSO, and weight scheduling adds nothing measurable.}

\keywords{Quantum-behaved particle swarm optimization, Attractor decomposition, Control experiments,
Weight scheduling, CEC2017, Feature selection}

\maketitle

% =======================================================================
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
Particle swarm optimization (PSO)~\cite{Kennedy1995} is prone to premature convergence on
multimodal landscapes. QPSO~\cite{Sun2004} replaces the velocity update by sampling from a
delta-potential-well distribution centered on a local attractor, which is a random convex
combination of a particle's personal best and the global best. Much QPSO work modifies this
attractor or adds an operator around it~\cite{Fang2010}. The usual evaluation then compares the
hybrid with QPSO as a whole, and this cannot show which change produced the difference.

BioQPSO, the method studied here, is a typical case. Its attractor,
\begin{equation}
q_{i,d}(t)=\phi_1\,p_{i,d}(t)+\phi_2\,g_d(t)+\phi_3\,b_{i,d}(t),\qquad
\phi_1+\phi_2+\phi_3=1,
\label{eq:attractor}
\end{equation}
differs from the QPSO attractor in at least three ways at once. It drops the random mixing
weight, it adds a ring-neighbor leader $b_i$, and $\phi_3$ may vary over time. The bee variant
also adds scout restarts. An earlier version of this work~\cite{Manav2026BioQPSO} compared the whole
method with baselines. This paper asks instead what each component contributes, and uses control
experiments to separate them.

The main findings are negative, and we report them as such. Removing the random weight costs
performance on the classical suite, leaders recover only part of what is lost, scouts at their default limit are
harmful, and scheduling $\phi_3$ gives no measurable benefit.

The contributions are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item An attractor decomposition of a QPSO hybrid into random weights, fixed weights, scouts, leader
 and schedule, with a control for each step on classical and CEC2017 functions
 (Table~\ref{tab:decomp}). % const
\item A test of whether a scheduled $\phi_3$ beats the best fixed value under a decision rule
 specified before the analysis, with the result that no schedule is credited on any function
 (Sections~\ref{sec:controls} and~\ref{sec:cec}).
\item A comparison of \EoneK{} algorithms in one implementation, including L-SHADE, on classical,
 shifted and CEC2017 functions, showing how far the ranking depends on the suite
 (Sections~\ref{sec:classical}--\ref{sec:cec}).
\item A test of the Schwefel failure of the BioQPSO family, which moves the optimum away from the
 bounds (Section~\ref{sec:schwefel}).
\item An honest account of the corrections made to earlier implementations, with public code and
 per-run results (Section~\ref{sec:protocol} and the Declarations).
\end{enumerate}

% =======================================================================
\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{The QPSO attractor.}
QPSO was introduced by Sun et al.~\cite{Sun2004}, and Fang et al.~\cite{Fang2010} review its variants.
Sun et al.\ analyze its convergence~\cite{Sun2012} and the behavior of individual particles,
including the choice of the contraction--expansion coefficient~\cite{SunEC2012}. Several
variants change the attractor itself: one draws it from a Gaussian distribution~\cite{Sun2011GA},
and a ring model has been used for multi-objective QPSO~\cite{Zhou2016}. Neither isolates the effect of
the random weight, which is the first step of our decomposition.

\paragraph{Neighborhoods and bio-inspired operators.}
Population structure affects PSO performance~\cite{KennedyMendes2002}, which motivates a ring
neighbor as a third anchor. Artificial bee colony (ABC)~\cite{Karaboga2007,KarabogaAkay2009} provides the
scout mechanism used in BeeBioQPSO, and ACO$_\mathbb{R}$~\cite{Socha2008} extends ant colony
optimization to continuous domains. S\"orensen~\cite{Sorensen2015} criticizes metaheuristics
justified mainly by their metaphor; our controls apply this criticism to our own method.

\paragraph{Scheduling.}
Time-varying parameters have a long history in PSO, for example time-varying acceleration
coefficients~\cite{Ratnaweera2004}. Adaptive QPSO work usually schedules the contraction--expansion
coefficient $\beta$, the step size of the sampling. The weight $\phi_3$ instead controls which anchor
guides the sample, and it exists only in the three-term form.

\paragraph{Benchmarking and center bias.}
Niu et al.~\cite{Niu2019} report that GWO performs better the closer an optimum is to the origin, and
Kudela~\cite{Kudela2022} discusses the wider problem of center-biased methods evaluated on
zero-centered benchmarks. Camacho-Villal\'on et al.~\cite{Camacho2023} examine GWO, WOA and four
other algorithms and call them misleading. We keep GWO~\cite{Mirjalili2014} and WOA~\cite{Mirjalili2016} as
baselines because of their wide use, and test the bias directly. L-SHADE~\cite{Tanabe2014} is included as a
strong differential evolution baseline.

% =======================================================================
\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
\subsection{QPSO}
For particle $i$ and dimension $d$,
\begin{equation}
x_{i,d}(t{+}1)=q_{i,d}(t)\pm\beta\,|m_d(t)-x_{i,d}(t)|\ln\frac1u,
\label{eq:qpso-position}
\end{equation}
with $+$ if $u\le0.5$ and $-$ otherwise, $u\sim U(0,1)$, and mean best % const
$m_d(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n p_{i,d}(t)$. The coefficient $\beta$ decreases linearly from 1.0 to 0.5. % const
Standard QPSO uses
\begin{equation}
q_{i,d}(t)=\varphi\,p_{i,d}(t)+(1-\varphi)\,g_d(t),\quad\varphi\sim U(0,1).
\label{eq:qpso-attractor}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Three-term attractor and leaders}
Eq.~(\ref{eq:attractor}) replaces Eq.~(\ref{eq:qpso-attractor}), with $p_i$ the personal best, $g$ the
global best and $b_i$ the leader of the ring neighborhood $\mathcal N_i=\{i-1,i,i+1\}$ (modular). % const

\paragraph{AntBioQPSO.}
Each particle keeps a pheromone value $\tau_i$, with evaporation $\tau_i\leftarrow(1-\rho)\tau_i$ each
iteration and deposit $\tau_i\leftarrow\tau_i+\Delta$ when its personal best improves. The leader is
the personal best of the neighbor with the most pheromone:
\begin{equation}
b_{i,d}=p_{\hat k,d},\qquad \hat k=\arg\max_{k\in\mathcal N_i}\tau_k .
\end{equation}

\paragraph{BeeBioQPSO.}
The leader is the best personal best in the neighborhood,
$\hat k=\arg\min_{k\in\mathcal N_i}f(p_k)$. Each particle has a stagnation counter $s_i$; if
$s_i>L_{\mathrm{scout}}$ it is re-initialized uniformly (a scout), and that evaluation counts toward the budget.

\subsection{Schedules for $\phi_3$}
We schedule $\phi_3(t)\in[\phi_3^{\min},\phi_3^{\max}]$ and keep the simplex constraint by distributing
the remainder in a fixed $4{:}3$ ratio:
\begin{equation}
\phi_1(t)=\tfrac47\bigl(1-\phi_3(t)\bigr),\qquad
\phi_2(t)=\tfrac37\bigl(1-\phi_3(t)\bigr).
\label{eq:redistribution}
\end{equation}
\emph{LinearAda} uses $\phi_3(t)=\phi_3^{\max}-(\phi_3^{\max}-\phi_3^{\min})\,t/T_{\max}$.
\emph{CosineAda} uses $\phi_3(t)=\phi_3^{\min}+\tfrac12(\phi_3^{\max}-\phi_3^{\min})\bigl(1+\cos(\pi t/T_{\max})\bigr)$.
\emph{FeedbackAda} uses a global stagnation counter $s_g$, reset when $g$ improves:
\begin{equation}
\phi_3(t{+}1)=\begin{cases}
\min(\phi_3(t)+\delta,\phi_3^{\max}), & s_g(t)>W,\\
\max(\phi_3(t)-\delta,\phi_3^{\min}), & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
\emph{PerParticleAda} uses each particle's own counter:
$\phi_{3,i}(t)=\phi_3^{\min}+(\phi_3^{\max}-\phi_3^{\min})\min(s_i/L_{\mathrm{scout}},1)$.
In the main comparison, the linear, cosine and feedback schedules use the ant leader and the
per-particle schedule uses the bee leader. The control experiment on classical functions runs every
schedule on both leaders, so schedule and leader type are not confounded there.

\subsection{The decomposition}\label{sec:decomp-def}
Each comparison changes one component:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Random to fixed weights:} no-bio control ($\phi_3=0$, $\phi_1{:}\phi_2=4{:}3$, ant variant, so % const
 no leader and no scouts) against QPSO.
\item \emph{Scouts:} bee no-bio control against ant no-bio control. The two differ only in scouts.
\item \emph{Leader:} fixed $\phi_3$ with leader against the no-bio control of the same variant.
\item \emph{Scheduling:} each schedule against the best fixed $\phi_3$ per function, and against the default.
 A random-$\phi_3$ control, redrawn each iteration, tests whether variation alone matters.
\end{enumerate}
Comparison 2 and the comparison with the default were not in the rule as first written and are % const
exploratory; the leader and best-fixed comparisons are the ones the rule governs.

\begin{algorithm}[!htbp]
\caption{Unified BioQPSO}\label{alg:main}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\State \textbf{Input:} $n$, bounds, $D$, $T_{\max}$, schedule, leader $\in\{$Ant, Bee$\}$
\State Initialize $x_i$ uniformly; $p_i\!\leftarrow\!x_i$; $g\!\leftarrow\!\arg\min f(p_i)$; $\tau_i\!\leftarrow\!1$; $s_i\!\leftarrow\!0$; $s_g\!\leftarrow\!0$
\For{$t=1$ \textbf{to} $T_{\max}$, while the budget lasts}
  \State compute $\phi_3(t)$ (or $\phi_{3,i}(t)$); set $\phi_1,\phi_2$ by Eq.~(\ref{eq:redistribution})
  \State $\beta\leftarrow\beta_{\mathrm{start}}-(\beta_{\mathrm{start}}-\beta_{\mathrm{end}})t/T_{\max}$; $m\leftarrow\frac1n\sum_i p_i$
  \State (Ant) $\tau_i\leftarrow(1-\rho)\tau_i$
  \For{each particle $i$}
    \State $b_i\leftarrow p_{\hat k}$ (Ant: max $\tau$; Bee: min $f(p_k)$ over $\mathcal N_i$)
    \State $q_i\leftarrow\phi_1p_i+\phi_2g+\phi_3b_i$
    \State sample $x_i$ by Eq.~(\ref{eq:qpso-position}); clip to bounds; evaluate $f_{\mathrm{new}}$
    \If{$f_{\mathrm{new}}<f(p_i)$}
      \State $p_i\!\leftarrow\!x_i$; update $g$; (Ant) $\tau_i\!\leftarrow\!\tau_i+\Delta$; $s_i\!\leftarrow\!0$
    \Else
      \State $s_i\leftarrow s_i+1$
    \EndIf
  \EndFor
  \State (Bee) re-initialize and evaluate particles with $s_i>L_{\mathrm{scout}}$; $s_i\leftarrow0$
  \State (Feedback) update $s_g$ and $\phi_3$
\EndFor
\State \Return $g$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Cost and convergence.}
A position update is $\mathcal O(nD)$ per iteration, pheromone and counter updates add $\mathcal
O(n)$, and scouts re-evaluate at most $n$ particles, so the total cost is $\mathcal O(nDT)$ as for
QPSO. For $\phi_k\ge0$ the attractor lies in the convex hull of $\{p_i,g,b_i\}$. This is a design
rationale. It does not show that the known QPSO convergence analysis~\cite{Sun2012} carries over, and no
proof is claimed.

\section{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
\subsection{Protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
\paragraph{Budget and seeds.}
Unless stated otherwise, $n=30$, $T_{\max}=1000$, 30 independent runs, $D=30$ and at most 30{,}030 % const
function evaluations (FEs). This is a light budget, since the CEC standard is $10^4 D$ FEs, so the CEC2017
experiments are also run at the standard budget (Section~\ref{sec:cec}). Seeds were fixed in advance
and shared, so all algorithms start from the same population for a given run index.

\paragraph{Functions.}
Ten classical functions (Table~\ref{tab:funcs}) are used in their standard form (E1) and with the optimum moved to % const
$o\sim U(0.8\,\mathrm{lb},0.8\,\mathrm{ub})^D$, redrawn per run, with the same bounds (E1b). % const
CEC2017~\cite{Awad2017} is evaluated with the official C code of the competition, called from Python, on its 29 functions, F1 and F3--F30 % const
(the organizers removed F2). An earlier run of this study used the opfunu library~\cite{opfunu}, which agrees with the official code on only % const
\CecOffSameCount{} of its functions; that run and the comparison are reported in Supplementary Section~\ref{S-sec:official} and are not used here.

\paragraph{Statistics.}
Primary inference is across functions: the Friedman test on mean ranks, with the Nemenyi critical difference
$\mathrm{CD}=q_{0.05}\sqrt{k(k+1)/(6N)}$~\cite{Demsar2006}, and Holm-corrected~\cite{Holm1979} Wilcoxon
tests on per-function means against QPSO. Ties receive average ranks. Per function, we use two-sided Wilcoxon
tests paired by seed, Holm-corrected across algorithms and with win/tie/loss counts; a relative difference
below 1\% counts as a tie. Effect sizes are matched-pairs rank-biserial $r$ with bootstrap 95\% CIs % const
(Supplementary Table~\ref{S-tab:eff}). Failure to separate two algorithms is not evidence that they are equivalent.

\paragraph{Decision rule.}
The decision rule was specified before the analysis. A component is credited
on a function if it beats its control under a one-sided Wilcoxon test, Holm-corrected over functions, at $p<0.05$ % const
with a relative improvement above 1\% (on $f-f^*$ for the classical functions, and on raw values on CEC2017, % const
as locked). It is credited overall on more than 5 of 10 classical functions, or at least 15 of 29 CEC2017 % const
functions. The dates matter here. The rule document is dated 2026-10-05, before the first experiment log of that % const
day, but its first version-controlled record is dated 2026-10-14, so that record alone does not prove the order. % const
The CEC2017 threshold was added on 2026-11-02, before any CEC2017 control result existed, and restated for the 29 official % const
functions on 2026-11-06, before any run on the official code. After the % const
rule was written, errors were found in the no-bio control and in baseline implementations, and the affected
experiments were re-run; all numbers here come from the corrected code. Results from before the
corrections had been seen, so the corrections were not blind. Every deviation from the rule, including the experiments added later,
is documented in the reproduction package.

\subsection{Classical functions (E1)}\label{sec:classical}
The Friedman test rejects equal ranks ($\chi^2=\EoneChi$, $p=\EoneP$, $k=\EoneK$, $N=\EoneN$;
Table~\ref{tab:ranks}). \EoneBestName{} ranks first (\EoneRankABC), then \EoneSecondName{} (\EoneRankLSHADE),
with GWO and WOA tied at \EoneRankGWO{} and QPSO at \EoneRankQPSO. No BioQPSO variant ranks above QPSO; the
best is AntBio at \EoneRankAntBio. With $\mathrm{CD}=\EoneCD$, no algorithm is separated from QPSO.
The best mean (Table~\ref{tab:classical}) is achieved by ABC on \EoneWinFnsABC; by WOA on \EoneWinFnsWOA; by L-SHADE on
\EoneWinFnsLSHADE; and by GWO on \EoneWinFnsGWO. Per function, AntBio wins, ties and loses against QPSO on
\EoneWAntBio, \EoneTAntBio{} and \EoneLAntBio{} functions, and BeeBio on \EoneWBeeBio, \EoneTBeeBio{} and \EoneLBeeBio{}
(Supplementary Table~\ref{S-tab:wtl}). Means can mislead on \EoneQpsoOutlierFns: QPSO has mean \EoneMeanLevyQPSO{} but median
\EoneMedLevyQPSO{} and maximum \EoneMaxLevyQPSO, so a few runs dominate its mean. Medians, interquartile ranges and standard deviations are in
Supplementary Section~\ref{S-sec:clfull} and Table~\ref{S-tab:clstd}. So on standard classical functions, the additions to the attractor do not improve on QPSO.

\subsection{Shifted functions (E1b)}\label{sec:shifted}
Moving the optimum changes the ranking sharply ($\chi^2=\EonebChi$, $p=\EonebP$, $\mathrm{CD}=\EonebCD$;
Tables~\ref{tab:ranks} and~\ref{tab:shifted}). GWO falls from \EoneRankGWO{} to \EonebRankGWO{} and WOA from
\EoneRankWOA{} to \EonebRankWOA, and they lose to QPSO on \EonebLGWO{} and \EonebLWOA{} of \EonebN{} functions. \EonebSepList{} are the algorithms
separated from QPSO, all in the worse direction ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=\EonebPwGWO$ on means for GWO and WOA).
ABC and L-SHADE share first place (\EonebRankABC), and QPSO is third (\EonebRankQPSO).
The best BioQPSO variant is Ant-Cos (\EonebRankAntCos).

\paragraph{Caveat on GWO and WOA.}
The strong E1 results of GWO and WOA therefore come from having the optimum at the origin: the same algorithms on
the same functions lose everywhere once it moves. This matches the center bias reported for GWO~\cite{Niu2019} and
for center-biased methods generally~\cite{Kudela2022}. Their E1 results should not be generalized. The same bias
may affect any algorithm, so E1b and CEC2017 carry more weight than E1 in what follows.

\subsection{Controls on classical functions (E2)}\label{sec:controls}
E2 runs both leaders with fixed $\phi_3\in\{0.1,\dots,0.5\}$, every schedule, the random-$\phi_3$ control, the no-bio % const
controls and QPSO. Table~\ref{tab:decomp} gives the decomposition, and Supplementary Section~\ref{S-sec:clfull} has the full sweep.

\paragraph{Random to fixed weights.}
With no leader and no scouts, fixed weights are better than QPSO on \DecBetterAnt{} functions and worse on
\DecWorseAnt{} (\DecWorseFnsAnt). Means include Zakharov \EtwoMeanZakharovAntNobio{} against
\EtwoMeanZakharovQPSO{} for QPSO, and Ackley \EtwoMeanAckleyAntNobio{} against \EtwoMeanAckleyQPSO. So the loss of the random
weight is the largest cost that BioQPSO pays on this suite, and it is a cost that the earlier comparisons could not show.

\paragraph{Scouts.}
Adding scouts to fixed weights is worse on \DcScoutsClWorse{} of \EoneN{} functions and better on \DcScoutsClBetter.
This cost is tied to the default limit $L_{\mathrm{scout}}$ (Section~\ref{sec:sens}).

\paragraph{Leaders.}
The ant leader is credited on \EtwoBioCountAnt{} of \EoneN{} functions (\EtwoBioFnsAnt), so it is not credited overall.
Under the rule the bee leader is credited overall, on \EtwoBioCountBee{} of \EoneN{} (\EtwoBioFnsBee). Neither is significantly
worse than its control on any function. Table~\ref{tab:bio} has the per-function results. Earlier text
claimed that the leader hurt on smooth functions, so we report them explicitly. The leader's mean against the no-bio mean is, for the ant and bee variants respectively:
Dixon--Price \EtwoMeanDixonPriceAntFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanDixonPriceAntNobio{} and \EtwoMeanDixonPriceBeeFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanDixonPriceBeeNobio;
Zakharov \EtwoMeanZakharovAntFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanZakharovAntNobio{} and \EtwoMeanZakharovBeeFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanZakharovBeeNobio;
Ackley \EtwoMeanAckleyAntFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanAckleyAntNobio{} and \EtwoMeanAckleyBeeFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanAckleyBeeNobio;
Sphere \EtwoMeanSphereAntFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanSphereAntNobio{} and \EtwoMeanSphereBeeFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanSphereBeeNobio;
Griewank \EtwoMeanGriewankAntFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanGriewankAntNobio{} and \EtwoMeanGriewankBeeFixed{} vs \EtwoMeanGriewankBeeNobio.
That earlier claim came from the faulty control and is withdrawn; none of these differences is significantly in the control's favor. The bee credit needs careful reading: its control carries the scouts, so the
leader recovers part of the scout damage, and BeeBio remains worse than QPSO on \DcNetBeeClWorse{} of \EoneN{} functions.
Among the five variants, mean ranks are QPSO \EtwoRankQPSO, AntBio \EtwoRankAntBio, ant no-bio \EtwoRankAntNobio,
BeeBio \EtwoRankBeeBio{} and bee no-bio \EtwoRankBeeNobio.

\paragraph{Scheduling.}
No schedule is credited on any function: \EtwoSchedTotal{} credits over \EtwoSchedN{} schedule--leader pairs and \EoneN{}
functions, for both leaders and the random-$\phi_3$ control. Schedules are significantly worse than the
per-function best fixed value in \EtwoSchedHarmTotal{} cells, although that baseline is chosen after the fact and so
favors the fixed setting. Against the plain default $\phi_3=0.3$, none is better on any function either % const
(Table~\ref{tab:decomp}), so there is no tuning effort for scheduling to save. The heat map in
Fig.~\ref{fig:phi3heat} shows why there is little to exploit: on \EtwoFlatCount{} of \EoneN{} functions (\EtwoFlatFns) all
fixed values lie within a factor of two (mean error, ant leader). For the bee leader, the larger values usually rank best, which fits the leader offsetting scout damage; for the ant leader no value dominates. % const

\subsection{CEC2017}\label{sec:cec}
\paragraph{Standard budget (E3s).}
At $10^4D$ FEs, Friedman gives $\chi^2=\EthreesThirtyChi$, $p=\EthreesThirtyP$ at $D=30$ and $\chi^2=\EthreesFiftyChi$, $p=\EthreesFiftyP$ at $D=50$, with $\mathrm{CD}=\EthreesThirtyCD$
(Table~\ref{tab:cecranks}; means in Supplementary Tables~\ref{S-tab:e3sa}--\ref{S-tab:e3s50b}).
L-SHADE ranks first at both dimensions (\EthreesThirtyRankLSHADE{} and \EthreesFiftyRankLSHADE), is the only algorithm separated from QPSO in its favor, and
against QPSO per function wins \EthreesThirtyWLSHADE{} and loses \EthreesThirtyLLSHADE{} of \EthreesThirtyN{} at $D=30$ (\EthreesFiftyWLSHADE{} and \EthreesFiftyLLSHADE{} at $D=50$).
PSO, GWO and WOA are the three worst at both dimensions and are separated from QPSO.

At $D=30$, \EthreesThirtyBioBetterCount{} BioQPSO variants rank above QPSO, and \EthreesFiftyBioBetterCount{} at $D=50$, with Ant-FB best (\EthreesThirtyRankAntFB{} and \EthreesFiftyRankAntFB;
QPSO \EthreesThirtyRankQPSO{} and \EthreesFiftyRankQPSO). The largest gaps, \EthreesThirtyBioGap{} and \EthreesFiftyBioGap{} ranks, are below CD. The Holm-corrected Wilcoxon test on means
finds \EthreesThirtyBioPwBetterList{} better than QPSO at $D=30$ ($p=\EthreesThirtyPwAntFB$) and \EthreesFiftyBioPwBetterList{} at $D=50$ ($p=\EthreesFiftyPwAntBio$ and $\EthreesFiftyPwAntFB$),
and no variant worse. As on the light budget, the two procedures disagree, and we report both. We treat this as weak evidence, not as an established difference, because it holds under one of the two procedures only.
Per function, AntBio wins \EthreesThirtyWAntBio{} and loses \EthreesThirtyLAntBio{} at $D=30$ and wins \EthreesFiftyWAntBio{} and loses \EthreesFiftyLAntBio{} at $D=50$; Ant-FB wins \EthreesThirtyWAntFB{} and loses \EthreesThirtyLAntFB{}
at $D=30$ and wins \EthreesFiftyWAntFB{} and loses \EthreesFiftyLAntFB{} at $D=50$. BeeBio loses \EthreesThirtyLBeeBio{} and \EthreesFiftyLBeeBio, and Bee-PP \EthreesThirtyLBeePP{} and \EthreesFiftyLBeePP.
On $f-f^*$ instead of raw values, AntBio wins \EthreesFiftyErrWAntBio{} and loses \EthreesFiftyErrLAntBio{} at $D=50$.
These are comparisons with QPSO alone: the standard budget has no controls, so they do not separate the leader from the fixed weights.

As a check of our L-SHADE, we compared it with the competition results of jSO~\cite{Brest2017jSO}, an improved L-SHADE, and of LSHADE-SPACMA~\cite{Mohamed2017LSHADESPACMA}
at the same budget (Supplementary Table~\ref{S-tab:lshade}). Our mean error lies within a factor of two of jSO's on \LsWithinTwoThirty{} of \LsFns{} functions at $D=30$ and
\LsWithinTwoFifty{} at $D=50$; the largest ratio is \LsMaxRatioThirty{} (\LsMaxRatioFnThirty{}, $D=30$), in jSO's favor.

\paragraph{Light budget (E3).}
Friedman gives $\chi^2=\EthreeChi$, $p=\EthreeP$ with $\mathrm{CD}=\EthreeCD$ (Table~\ref{tab:cecranks}). L-SHADE ranks first
(\EthreeRankLSHADE), then AntBio (\EthreeRankAntBio), Ant-FB (\EthreeRankAntFB), BeeBio and Ant-Cos (\EthreeRankBeeBio), and QPSO is at \EthreeRankQPSO.
So \EthreeBioBetterCount{} BioQPSO variants rank above QPSO, but the largest gap is \EthreeMaxGap{} and below CD, and none differs from QPSO on means
(AntBio: $p=\EthreePwAntBio$). L-SHADE's gap to QPSO is also below CD, yet the Wilcoxon test on means is significant ($p=\EthreePwLSHADE$), so the two procedures disagree there.
GWO (\EthreeRankGWO) and WOA (\EthreeRankWOA) are the worst and the only algorithms separated from QPSO, consistent with E1b. Supplementary Tables~\ref{S-tab:ceca} and~\ref{S-tab:cecb} give the means.

\paragraph{Controls on CEC2017 (E2c).}
E2c repeats the controls at the light budget (Table~\ref{tab:decomp}, and Supplementary Tables~\ref{S-tab:ceccontrols} and~\ref{S-tab:biocec}). On this suite, the cost of
fixed weights almost disappears: better than QPSO on \DcRandomToFixedCeBetter{} functions and worse on \DcRandomToFixedCeWorse.
Scouts at the default limit are worse on \DcScoutsCeWorse{} of \EthreeN{} functions and better on \DcScoutsCeBetter, a smaller cost than on the classical suite.
The ant leader is credited on \EtwocBioCountAnt{} functions (\EtwocBioFnsAnt) and the bee leader on \EtwocBioCountBee{} (\EtwocBioFnsBee), below the threshold of 15, % const
so neither is credited overall, and neither is significantly worse than its control on any function. The bee credits are again measured against a control that carries
the scouts: BeeBio is better than QPSO on \DcNetBeeCeBetter{} functions and worse on \DcNetBeeCeWorse. No schedule is credited on any function
(\EtwocSchedTotal{} over \EtwocSchedN{} schedules), against the best of three fixed values. Mean ranks among the five variants are AntBio \EtwocRankAntBio, BeeBio \EtwocRankBeeBio,
QPSO \EtwocRankQPSO, ant no-bio \EtwocRankAntNobio{} and bee no-bio \EtwocRankBeeNobio.
The rule's raw-value form is strict on CEC2017, whose offsets inflate the denominator. Using $f-f^*$ instead gives \EtwocErrBioCountAnt{} and \EtwocErrBioCountBee{}
credits, still below the threshold.

\subsection{The Schwefel failure (E7, E7b)}\label{sec:schwefel}
All BioQPSO variants fail on Schwefel in E1, while QPSO does less badly (\EsevQPSOClip{} against \EsevAntBioClip{} for AntBio and
\EsevBeeBioClip{} for BeeBio). The leader is not the cause, since the no-bio control is also poor (\EsevnobioantClip). Reflecting at the
bounds helps QPSO strongly (\EsevQPSOReflect) and BeeBio moderately (\EsevBeeBioReflect), but AntBio little (\EsevAntBioReflect), and random re-initialization
makes all of them worse (Table~\ref{tab:e7}).

E7b moves the optimum inward, from $c=420.97$ to $c=120.97$, to test whether the gap exists because the optimum lies near the bound % const
(Supplementary Section~\ref{S-sec:e7b}). Under clipping, \EsevBWorseNear{} of 6 family members are significantly worse than QPSO with the optimum near % const
the bound and \EsevBWorseInward{} with it inward, but under reflection the gap remains (AntBio's ratio to QPSO's mean, \EsevBRatioNearReflectAnt{} near and
\EsevBRatioInwardReflectAnt{} inward). The hypothesis therefore holds for clipping, the handling used in the main experiments, but does not fully explain the failure.

\subsection{Scalability (E4)}\label{sec:scal}
E4 uses $D\in\{30,50,100\}$, six functions, seven algorithms, 30 runs and $10^4 D$ FEs, which is \EfourJobs{} runs in total % const
(Fig.~\ref{fig:scal}, Table~\ref{tab:scal}). Mean ranks are close at the larger budget: at $D=30$, QPSO \EfourRankThirtyQPSO, Ant-FB \EfourRankThirtyAntFB,
AntBio \EfourRankThirtyAntBio{} and GWO \EfourRankThirtyGWO; at $D=100$, QPSO and GWO \EfourRankHundredQPSO, AntBio \EfourRankHundredAntBio{} and Ant-FB
\EfourRankHundredAntFB. The bee variants are last at every dimension (\EfourRankHundredBeeBio{} and \EfourRankHundredBeePP{} at $D=100$). QPSO has the best mean on
\EfourWinFnsHundredQPSO{} at every dimension, and AntBio on \EfourWinFnsHundredAntBio{} at $D=100$. GWO's exact zeros on \EfourGwoZeroFns{} at all dimensions fit the
origin bias of Section~\ref{sec:shifted}, as these functions are not shifted. So no BioQPSO variant scales better than QPSO overall. Only the ant variants stay level with it.

\subsection{Feature selection (E8)}\label{sec:fs}
Each particle is a vector in $[0,1]^D$, and entries of at least 0.5 select a feature. Fitness is % const
$f(x)=0.7(1-\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{inner}})+0.3|S|/D$ with 5-fold inner cross-validation on the outer-training split. % const
Features are standardized on the outer-training split. Outer folds are stratified 5-fold repeated six times (30 % const
evaluations per algorithm and dataset), and test accuracy uses $k$-NN and an RBF SVM. % const
The datasets are Breast Cancer and Wine from scikit-learn, and Ionosphere and Madelon from OpenML. Runs use 30 particles and 1,530 FEs, or 630 FEs on Madelon. % const
The baselines are all features and mutual-information top-$k$ with $k=\lfloor D/4\rfloor$. L-SHADE is not included: this experiment predates its addition, and its initial population of $18D$ would exceed Madelon's budget. % const

Selection does not help on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:fs}). All features give the best accuracy with both classifiers on \FsAllBeatsList,
where all \FsBCKnnBelowAll{} selectors are significantly below them, and mutual-information top-$k$ also beats every selector on \FsMiBeatsList.
On Ionosphere the result depends on the classifier: selection lifts $k$-NN from \FsIonoKnnAll{} to \FsIonoKnnBest{} (\FsIonoKnnBestName), while the SVM is best with all features (\FsIonoSvmAll).
Madelon is the only dataset where selection helps both classifiers: \FsMadKnnBestName{} reaches \FsMadKnnBest{} and \FsMadSvmBest{} against \FsMadKnnAll{} and \FsMadSvmAll{} for all features.
Against QPSO, only \FsCreditTotal{} of \FsCells{} comparisons is a significant gain above 0.005 (\FsMadKnnCredited, Madelon, $k$-NN), \FsBioCreditTotal{} involve a BioQPSO variant, and \FsWorseTotal{} are significantly below QPSO. % const
Subsets are small on the three smaller datasets, for example \FsBCFeatQpso{} of 30 features for QPSO on Breast Cancer, because the fitness rewards small subsets; part of the accuracy lost there is that trade-off. % const
On Madelon, QPSO still keeps \FsMadFeatQpso{} of 500 features at this budget, whereas WOA keeps \FsMadFeatWoa{} with lower accuracy. % const
These results give no support to a BioQPSO variant for feature selection at these budgets.

\subsection{Runtime (E9)}\label{sec:runtime}
Table~\ref{tab:runtime} gives the cost per 1,000 FEs at $D=30$ over \RtFns{} classical functions (Sphere, Rastrigin, Levy, Schwefel), as the median over functions of the median of 10 runs of 30,030 FEs, in one process on an otherwise idle Apple M4. % const
Costs range from \RtLo{} ms (L-SHADE) to \RtHi{} ms (ACO$_\mathbb{R}$), with QPSO at \RtQpso{} ms. AntBio is \RtOverAntBio{} \RtDirAntBio{} than QPSO, and schedules add almost nothing: the fixed, linear, cosine and feedback ant variants lie within \RtAntSpread.
GWO is \RtOverGWO{} \RtDirGWO{} than QPSO, although both have the same $\mathcal O(nDT)$ cost and the same number of evaluations. A profile on Sphere shows that its random-number generation takes \RtProfGwoRng{} of its time against \RtProfQpsoRng{} for QPSO, because each wolf draws six random vectors, and its per-agent update steps take \RtProfGwoSelf{} (QPSO: \RtProfQpsoSelf). The gap is therefore a matter of our implementation, not of the algorithm. % const
A first pass that ran the algorithms in sequence gave a ratio of \RtSeqRatio{} between two ant variants of equal cost on Rastrigin, so we interleaved them in random order and report that pass. These differences would be small next to any costly objective.

\subsection{Convergence}\label{sec:conv}
Figure~\ref{fig:conv} shows median error against FEs for eight algorithms. GWO and WOA fall fastest on the functions with the optimum at the origin, in
line with Section~\ref{sec:shifted}. BeeBio stalls at a higher error than AntBio on Sphere, Griewank, Ackley and Levy, which fits the cost of scouts in Table~\ref{tab:decomp}.
L-SHADE improves slowly at first and is still improving at the end of the budget on most functions, so the light budget penalizes it; this is one reason for the standard-budget CEC2017 runs.

\subsection{Sensitivity (E6)}\label{sec:sens}
One-at-a-time sweeps over five values of each parameter, on six classical and four CEC2017 functions, are in Supplementary Section~\ref{S-sec:sens}. % const
Of \EsixCells{} Holm-corrected Friedman tests, \EsixSigCells{} are significant: \EsixSigLscout{} for $L_{\mathrm{scout}}$, \EsixSigBeta{} for the $\beta$ range,
\EsixSigBounds{} for the $\phi_3$ bounds and \EsixSigRho{} for $\rho$, $W$ and $\delta$. The deposit $\Delta$ has no effect by construction: all \EsixDeltaTuples{} runs are identical
across its values, because scaling every deposit leaves the comparison between neighbors unchanged. The longest scout limit tested, \EsixLscoutMax, gives the best mean on
\EsixLscoutBestAtMax{} of \EsixFns{} functions (Sphere \EsixLSphereDefault{} at the default \EsixLscoutDefault{} against \EsixLSphereLong), so the cost of scouts belongs to
the default limit, not to scouts as such. We keep the frozen default, since choosing a limit here would tune on the test functions.

% =======================================================================
\section{Discussion}\label{sec:disc}
\paragraph{What the evidence supports.}
Within the attractor, the components act differently. Removing the random weight costs performance on classical functions and
little on CEC2017. Scouts are harmful on both suites at the default limit, and that cost shrinks as the limit grows (Section~\ref{sec:sens}). A ring-neighbor leader never significantly hurts relative to its control, and helps on a few
functions; only the bee leader on the classical suite passes the overall threshold, and it does so against a control already damaged by scouts.
Scheduling gives nothing, either against the best fixed value or against the default. Separately, GWO's and WOA's classical results depend on the optimum's location. In feature selection, the baselines match or beat the selectors on most dataset and classifier pairs, and no BioQPSO variant gains on QPSO.
At the standard CEC2017 budget, L-SHADE is clearly best. No BioQPSO variant is worse than QPSO on function means, and some ant-leader variants are better under one of the two procedures at both dimensions. This is the strongest positive result for the three-term attractor, and it is weak evidence only.

\paragraph{What it does not support.}
It does not support a claim that any BioQPSO variant is separated from QPSO by the Nemenyi test on any suite, or better than QPSO on the classical suite. Nor does it support crediting the ant leader overall, or
the claim that scheduling removes the need for tuning. The gain of the ant variants at the standard budget comes without controls, so it cannot be assigned to the leader rather than to the fixed weights, and it holds under one procedure only.

\paragraph{Practical recommendation.}
For a new continuous problem, start with L-SHADE: it ranks first at the standard CEC2017 budget at both dimensions and loses to QPSO on no function. If a simple swarm method with few parameters is wanted, QPSO is a sound default.
AntBioQPSO costs about \RtOverAntBio{} more time per evaluation and shows weak evidence of a small gain on CEC2017 at the standard budget, but it is not better on the classical suite.
Avoid GWO and WOA unless the optimum is known to lie near the center of the domain. Do not use scouts with a short stagnation limit, and do not expect a $\phi_3$ schedule to replace tuning.
For feature selection, compare against all features and a simple filter before using any metaheuristic.

\paragraph{Threats to validity.}
\emph{Budget:} the light budget favors fast early convergence, and leader credits were measured only there, as the standard-budget runs include no controls.
\emph{Tuning:} the bio-inspired settings were chosen in earlier work on the same functions, which may favor them, and some baseline settings are study choices or rest on secondary sources.
\emph{Scouts and budget:} scout evaluations count, so bee variants complete fewer iterations and their $\beta$ does not reach its final value, which is part of the measured cost of scouts.
\emph{Controls:} the scout comparison and the comparison with the default $\phi_3$ are exploratory, and CEC2017 fixed sweeps use three values rather than five. % const
\emph{Instances:} the CEC2017 results use the official code. A first run on the opfunu library, which differs from the official code in data or formula on all but \CecOffSameCount{} of its functions, is reported in the supplement only; where its conclusions differ, the official results govern.
\emph{Statistics:} \EoneN{} and \EthreeN{} functions give limited power, and 30 runs do not fully describe heavy tails such as Levy for QPSO. Outer folds in feature selection share data, so those $p$-values are optimistic.
\emph{Sensitivity:} one-at-a-time sweeps miss interactions, and the scout limit was not tested beyond \EsixLscoutMax.
\emph{Implementation:} earlier code contained errors; the current code was checked against the original papers and a reference implementation, and the checks that do not support a change are also reported.
WOA follows the reference code where it differs from the paper's notation.
\emph{Order of the rule:} the document date, which is not tamper-evident, is the only evidence that the rule preceded the first experiments.

% =======================================================================
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
We decomposed a three-term QPSO attractor with a control for each component. Fixed weights lose to QPSO's random weight on classical functions, scouts at their default limit are harmful on both suites, and
ring-neighbor leaders help on few functions, with no overall credit on CEC2017. Scheduling the leader weight is credited on no function.
At the standard CEC2017 budget L-SHADE is best, and there is weak evidence that some ant-leader variants beat QPSO on function means.
The classical strength of GWO and WOA disappears when the optimum moves, and feature selection favors no BioQPSO variant.
For QPSO hybrids, the lesson is to test each change against a control, because a whole-method comparison hides costs and benefits that act in opposite directions.
